entry.title: Modi at 25: Small signs, big challenge
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Modi at 25: Small signs, big challengeModi at 25: Small signs, big challenge

Multiple headwinds make the turbulence Mr Modi is battling as he steps into his 26th year in public office. This has brought the three-point Modi proposition under the greatest pressure since 2014

Prime Minister Narendra Modi (Image: Bloomberg)

Shekhar Gupta7 min read Last Updated : Oct 10 2026 | 9:30 AM ISTThis is the season of looking at Narendra Modi’s 25 years in power and beyond. His followers are celebrating. His Cabinet has passed a resolution praising him. Of course, the critics are out dissecting his quarter-century in public life, not with a scalpel but with a scythe. It’s also the season for people, especially journalists, telling their “when I first met Modi” stories. I’ll hold on to mine for another day. Let’s not risk diluting today’s serious argument. Two weeks ago, we noted that for any incumbent in India, the third year of a term is the toughest. This is when challenges build up, fatigue sets in, aspiring successors sharpen the knives. We also said that the last of these doesn’t apply to Mr Modi. Nobody in his party would even dare to whisper the “S” word.  The third year of Mr Modi’s third term, however, is beset with all of the other challenges. His tired and incomplete Cabinet is struggling. His chief ministers — barring Yogi Adityanath, Devendra Fadnavis and Himanta Biswa Sarma — aren’t up to the multiple challenges. Having used the ancient editorial privilege of ‘tabooing’ a word, and listing the cliched “narrative” under it, I then can’t use it. The fact is, this market of popular opinion is rife with competing, contradictory notions. The Modi-BJP story is still the most significant. It just isn’t as dominant as before. Multiple breezes make the turbulence Mr Modi is battling as he steps into his 26th year in public office. 

Also Read

Jaishankar holds talks with Ethiopian counterpart; discusses trade

Back to the future: Can Kolkata's iconic trams make a grand comeback?premium

Ruling parties sweep bypolls in Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, Assam, Puducherry

The making of brand Shashi Tharoorpremium

When the crops wiltpremium

This has brought the classical — and so far all-conquering — three-point Modi proposition under the greatest pressure since 2014. The three points are: Hard, Hinduised nationalism; ever-expanding welfare, distributed efficiently, with minimal friction or leakage; and visible construction of physical infrastructure. All of this without significant overhang of corruption. The Modi proposition survives. It’s just that several other factors have now emerged. And we aren’t just talking about the rebellion of an irreverential, ageist, educated and mostly not-impoverished GenZ.  What makes this period of crisis unprecedented in Mr Modi’s prime ministership is the convergence of these factors.. Like the Shakespearean “when sorrows come, they come not single spies, but in battalions.” In isolation, each of these factors may look small. But they become formidable when the big picture comes together. As the great management guru late C K Prahalad used to say: “Weak signals add up to a big change.” He elaborated this in his oft-quoted 1995 paper “Weak Signals Versus Strong Paradigms” (Sage Journals). Prahalad himself summarised it thus: “Taken one at a time, these signals don’t add up to much. But taken together, they present a picture of a country (or industry) in dramatic transformation.” Is this what Mr Modi is confronted with now? Let’s check out some facts. I am reducing these “battalions of sorrows” to a dozen most significant. 1. Dramatic damage to the credibility of the Election Commission of India (ECI), and thereby growing doubts over the integrity of the election process. 2. A growing belief that the top judiciary either doesn’t dare look the executive in the eye, or gives wishy-washy orders. Worse, that it speaks with a forked tongue. Ironically, this view is shared on both sides. 3. A solitary retired civil servant (Subhash Chandra Garg) has triggered a nationwide debate on the credibility of gross domestic product figures. 4. Inflation, as now forecast by the RBI, is set to rise to its highest level in nearly three years, and the rupee is struggling despite a highly successful, if expensive, dollar-deposit scheme. 5. Two of this establishment’s most trusted civil servants, the two Election Commissioners (ECs), protected their own backs by creating a paper trail to record their opposition to the Chief Election Commissioner’s decisions. 6. Ability of the Opposition, especially Rahul Gandhi, to lay siege to the Capital with English TV channels and Hindi newspapers, including the ones ‘most trusted’ by the establishment, giving it prominent airtime. 7. Young people lampooning the Prime Minister with mere feckless pushback from his “Right-wing” supporters, and an overnight phenomenon like CJP setting the agenda, from Neet to the state of government schools. 8. A small ally like Chirag Paswan taking a swipe at Bihar government over law and order. And a way smaller ally, Om Prakash Rajbhar, going public with his purported conversation with the Prime Minister on Uttar Pradesh’s division into multiple states, which Yogi Adityanath firmly opposes. 9. Contrary to the Modi government’s decisive image, we’ve seen festering indecisiveness —whether to press ahead with delimitation, or what to do with a Parliament session that has not been prorogued even two months after its adjournment sine die. To the naked eye, it shows a lack of confidence in marshalling the numbers for constitutional amendments the BJP really wants.  10. Inability, one can also add prolonged hesitation in carrying out a Cabinet reshuffle, or at least filling the vacant slots. There are too many of them, including education. 11. Continued value destruction in the stock market across Mr Modi’s third term, even as all global peers, from the US and Europe to Japan, South Korea, China and even Pakistan, have boomed. The disinclination to acknowledge the challenge is a self-destructive cop-out when millions from the middle class have moved their savings into systematic investment plans and are celebrated by the government for doing so. It also amounts to them having given the fleeing foreign portfolio investors (FPI), a golden handshake. 12. And finally, a global situation for India not seen in decades. Donald Trump has narrowed India’s strategic space in many areas. He’s also challenging our claims to strategic autonomy, with a provocation a day. Beyond Mr Trump, the war in Ukraine, smouldering West Asia, roiled energy markets, and a newly opened strategic-rentier window for Pakistan. All of these have come on top of a deficient monsoon. That’s beyond any government’s control. But these simmering discontents will play out in a below-average farming year. The larger issues, however, are rooted in the three most fundamental factors that have made India cohesive, and stronger over the decades. These are trust in the Constitution and the belief that nobody can take it away, fairness of the top judiciary, and independence of the Election Commission. All three are under strain now. The BJP knows better than its opponents how badly it was damaged in 2024 by rumours fed by just the odd statement from its middling functionaries and the Ayodhya candidate that the party needed 400 seats to change the Constitution. Now most Indians have not read the Constitution, or even the 106 amendments already carried out. But they see the Constitution almost like a deity or a scripture. Fair, secular, a bill of rights they won’t let anybody take away. Constant talk of special Parliament sessions have brought back these suspicions. The Supreme Court has unfortunately built a well-deserved reputation of flip-flops, cynical prevarications, and talking more than writing. This also applies to its treatment of the SIR issue so far. It’s being watched closely now as it battles multiple challenges—from restoring the credibility of the ECI to taking a view on the right to protest in the Capital. And finally, the ECI. Through nearly eight decades, the institution has had good days and bad, and some indifferent ones. It was, however, never as broken as it is now. An ECI caught in an every-man-for-himself trap will struggle to win back popular confidence. It’s a national crisis. These are the challenges Mr Modi needs to address as he steps into his 26th unbroken year in public office. If he doesn’t, or fails to do so, C.K. Prahalad’s small signals could lead to a dramatic crisis over a very painful two and a half years until the summer of 2029.

Elon Musk | Image: Bloomberg

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 10 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page.  Examples of oligarchs crying foul cannot be more ironic than Elon Musk accusing Indian tycoons of blocking Starlink. The resistance, however, stems primarily from the government’s security concerns, not Mukesh Ambani or Sunil Mittal, argues R Jagannathan. Satellite communications could help insurgents evade internet shutdowns, while Musk’s political activism and influence abroad raise concerns about foreign interference. The commercial market will initially be limited, with government agencies, businesses and wealthy users likelier customers than poor rural communities. With domestic alternatives being developed, Jagannathan argues that India must retain sovereign control over critical communications infrastructure and deny Musk a satellite licence.  Maharashtra’s deficient monsoon threatens the rabi crop, raising fears of a drought potentially worse than that of 1972. That earlier crisis prompted employment guarantees, food distribution reforms and measures to protect landless labourers. The 2026 Drought Management Code, however, appears inconsistently implemented, with some relatively well-watered areas qualifying for relief while others facing severe shortages are excluded. The resulting scramble for drought relief has become a contest over political patronage and constituency interests, observes Aditi Phadnis. The government’s once-dominant narrative of nationalism, welfare delivery and infrastructure development now competes with growing public discontent, notes Shekhar Gupta. He identifies 12 warning signs, including doubts over electoral integrity, judicial credibility, economic performance, government indecision, youth disaffection and shrinking strategic space under Donald Trump. The deeper crisis, he contends, concerns trust in the Constitution, the Supreme Court’s fairness and the Election Commission’s independence. After losing the race to become UN Secretary-General, Tharoor entered Indian politics, where his polished English initially attracted controversy but eventually became his signature asset. His 2017 use of “farrago” went viral, spawning memes and a Word of the Day following. Goyal sees this as a lesson in brand differentiation: standing apart can generate visibility more effectively than imitating rivals. Yet Tharoor’s linguistic flair also risks caricature, forcing him to demonstrate that his appeal extends beyond vocabulary to broader political substance and relevance.

entry.title: The making of brand Shashi Tharoor
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The making of brand Shashi TharoorThe making of brand Shashi Tharoor

The story of the man who makes you open a dictionary before breakfast is a masterclass in accidental differentiation

premium

Mr Tharoor’s brand lesson is simple: In a cluttered market, don’t try to be louder in the same language. Try to be different in a language only you can own (Photo:PTI)

Sandeep Goyal5 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 11:40 PM ISTIn India, there are two types of politicians. Type A: Those who rabble-rouse and make you clap or cry. Type B: Those who make you scratch your head and think. In a fun kind of way.   Shashi Tharoor single-handedly created Type B. And then made Type B more famous than Type A.  Ten years ago, he was a second-rung Congress MP from Thiruvananthapuram, known in Lutyens’ circles as “that UN guy who almost became Secretary General”. Respected, erudite, but not exactly someone your driver would discuss. Today, your driver knows him. Your cook knows him. Your 16-year-old knows him because he had to Google “sesquipedalian” after Mr Tharoor posted it on social media.  How did a diplomat with Oxford English become a mass brand in a country that loves three-word slogans? That’s Brand Tharoor. And it’s a masterclass in accidental differentiation. Mr Tharoor’s brand started in failure.  In 2006, he was India’s candidate for United Nations Secretary General. Shashi Tharoor vs Ban Ki-moon. He lost. Mr Tharoor should have won — suave, brilliant, author of five books, perfect UN English. But he didn’t. Most others would have retired to write columns.   Mr Tharoor did the opposite. He came back to India and joined politics — the one profession in India where good English is usually a disqualification.  In 2009, the Congress gave him Thiruvananthapuram. He won. Became minister of state for external affairs. Then came the first tweet that almost ended him. “Will travel in cattle class in solidarity with holy cows.” Talking about economy class. India erupted. In 2009, Twitter (now X) had 200,000 users in India. All of them were outraged. The headlines screamed: “Tharoor insults economy class passengers, calls them cattle.” He apologised.   But the brand was born — the English-speaking, slightly elitist, very witty man. Brand Tharoor pivoted from politician to phenomenon.  The real launch of Brand Tharoor was not a speech. It was a word. In July 2017, he tweeted: “Exasperating farrago of distortions, misrepresentations and outright lies.” India stopped. News anchors who had never used the word “farrago” in 20 years had to say it 20 times that evening. Memes exploded. School kids asked teachers — “What is farrago?”  And then Mr Tharoor did the smartest thing a brand can do — he owned it. He didn’t say: “Sorry for big words.” He launched “Tharoor’s Word of the Day.”  Farrago. Rodomontade. Sesquipedalian. Floccinaucinihilipilification — 29 letters, meaning the “act of estimating something as worthless”. He used it to describe something as worthless, using a word worthless to estimate worthlessness. Suddenly, every Indian who wanted to sound smart had a new guru. English teachers loved him. Tinder bios started saying: “Looking for someone who understands Tharoor without dictionary.”  This is classic brand differentiation. In a market where every politician was trying to be more desi, more simple, Mr Tharoor went the opposite way —  more complex, more English, more Oxford.  Byron Sharp would call it Distinctive Asset. In a sea of white kurta, Hindi slogan sameness, one man in a well-cut suit saying “snollygoster” stands out. You may not like him, but you cannot ignore him.  His English didn’t make him elite. It made him meme-able. In India today, meme-able is electable — at least for mindshare. From 2017 to 2020, Mr Tharoor became India’s most followed politician after Narendra Modi and Rahul Gandhi, without being Prime Minister, without being chief minister, without a single Hindi slogan. That’s not politics. That’s branding.  He turned vocabulary into virality.  The big words have both built and boxed him. For his fans, the words are proof of erudition. For his critics, the words are proof of elitism.  Mr Tharoor’s brand lesson is simple: In a cluttered market, don’t try to be louder in the same language. Try to be different in a language only you can own.  He didn’t try to out-Modi Modi in Hindi oratory. He didn’t try to out-Rahul Rahul in yatra. He owned English, books, wit — assets no one else could copy.  Second lesson: One distinctive word can be bigger than 100 speeches. Farrago did more for Mr Tharoor than 10 years of parliamentary questions.  Third lesson: Every strength, if overused, becomes your caricature. Mr Tharoor’s English got him famous, but now he has to work twice as hard to remind people he is more than English.  Brand Tharoor is not perfect. But it is lovable. In a country of 1.4 billion where most politicians sound the same, a man who makes you open a dictionary before breakfast has already won.  After all, as Mr Tharoor himself would say — his career is not an exasperating farrago, but a compelling case of rodomontade turned into relevance.  And you just Googled rodomontade, didn’t you?  That's Brand Tharoor.

entry.title: When the crops wilt
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / When the crops wiltWhen the crops wilt

The drought is almost providential for the ruling party as it postpones the hour of reckoning

premium

Seventy-five per cent of the state is officially stricken by drought and 82 per cent of agriculture is rain-fed with just 18 per cent irrigated area

Aditi Phadnis5 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 11:22 PM ISTIf it doesn’t rain in a few weeks, the rabi (winter-spring) agricultural season will also fail, and Maharashtra could be on the edge of a catastrophe after more than an 18 per cent deficiency in rain during the kharif (monsoon) season. Seventy-five per cent of the state is officially stricken by drought and 82 per cent of agriculture is rain-fed with just 18 per cent irrigated area.  Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis said last month: “We are bracing for severe drought, which could be worse than in 1972.” Revenue Minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule warned workers in Nagpur last month that “as the drought progresses, a bigger crisis will come upon Maharashtra. In fact, it will be bigger than the pandemic. There will be a shortage of water and fodder. You will see kharif and rabi wrecked. All crops will take a hit”. National Congress Party (SP) chief Sharad Pawar repeated the apprehension: “This year’s drought could be worse than in 1972.”  What happens to politics in a drought? Typically, it works out best for the ruling party. Take Mr Pawar. In terms of career progression, 1972 was not at all bad for him. He became a member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) for the first time from Baramati, and at 32, a state minister in charge of home and general administration in the Vasantrao Naik government. He was sent to other states to secure foodgrain for Maharashtra (he got a cold reception, he writes in his autobiography, from Uttar Pradesh because he refused to touch then chief minister Kamalapati Tripathi’s feet) but many other governments helped Maharashtra out. This eventually led to his star rising.  That 1972 drought was key to teaching India how to manage drought and food shortages. Maharashtra launched the Employment Guarantees Scheme (EGS) in 1969, the first state in India to do so. Research by economist Jean Dreze suggests that the poorest of the poor — agricultural landless labour — who were always the worst-hit in famines, found themselves relatively secure as a result of state intervention. The EGS provided this group a steady source of income and when, combined with the state’s robust public distribution system in the state, Maharashtra prevented the devastation that states like Bihar faced. True, the quality of the work and low payment, the quality of consumption, and the sudden injection of cash-fuelled consumption in a struggling rural economy had its own impact. But as economist Elizabeth Oughton observed in her research, some landless agricultural labour families “enjoyed” the drought because of the guarantee of work it represented.  More policy reform followed. Though only a junior minister, Mr Pawar scrapped the ban on the inter-district movement of fodder. Much later, came the construction of check dams (tiny dams built on nallahs) in the Prithviraj Chavan government (2009), cattle camps run by non-government organisations, and eventually the Drought Management Code (DMC) of 2026.  Although the DMC is rigorous in defining drought, its rollout apparently is not so much. Mahabaleshwar is one of the wettest towns in India. Yet it is on the list of talukas hit by drought and, therefore, eligible for drought relief. How could that happen? Although Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde represents an Assembly constituency in Thane, he belongs to the Mahabaleshwar taluka. And if every farmer — for instance — gets drought relief of ₹1 lakh per hectare and other benefits, so will farmers in Mahabaleshwar! By contrast, Kagal (represented by Hasan Mushrif in Kolhapur district), Shirdi (represented by Radhakant Vikhe Patil in Ahmadnagar district) and Dindori (represented by Narhari Zirwal in Nashik), among others, do not figure on the list, although all three are battling a severe shortage of water and crop failure. All three individuals belong to parties that are in the ruling alliance and are furious that their regions will not be eligible for drought relief.  So power, patronage and money fuel politics in drought: And the ruling party controls all of those. Climate-change activists can scream El Nino till they’re blue in the face. But the fact is, no one in Maharashtra is talking about “differences” between Mr Fadnavis and Mr Shinde for the moment. Instead, there is a wild scramble to get your constituency put on the drought-relief list. Crisis forces unity. In 1972, a young Sharad Pawar saw thousands of women led by Mrinal Gore, Ahilya Rangnekar and others take out the Laatni (rolling pin) morchas (processions) on Bombay streets, protesting against skyrocketing prices, beating empty tins with kitchen ladles.  All that is passe now.  In some ways, the drought is providential because it postpones the hour of reckoning in Maharashtra politics. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has no objection in principle to Mr Shinde, a Maratha, becoming chief minister. In fact, it badly needs a Maratha. But it would like him to merge his party, the Shiv Sena, into the BJP. Sena MLAs are against that move. Having won the Assembly elections and the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation polls pretty much on his own, Mr Fadnavis knows he is secure. But his followers and supporters are nudging him towards higher ambitions. A good drought is all things to all people!   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Musk is not worth pandering to
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Musk is not worth pandering toMusk is not worth pandering to

India has good reason to keep satellite communications under the control of operators subject to Indian laws and security oversight

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

R Jagannathan6 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 11:14 PM ISTExamples of the pot calling the kettle black do not get more egregious than this. On Thursday, October 8, SpaceX’s trillionaire boss, Elon Musk, who can surely be called the super-oligarch among tech oligarchs, claimed that his Starlink satellite phone services were being blocked by India’s oligarchs.  He said on his social media platform X: “Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people… you can guess who they are…. This is a crime against the people of India”. An X account linked to Mr Musk went on to talk about how over 11,256 villages are without even 4G services as of May 2026. Rahul Gandhi, currently engaged in climbing barricades and protesting “vote chori”, unwisely appeared to endorse Mr Musk’s claim, with a “Welcome to India” post. The last thing one needs is an Indian politician batting for a foreign oligarch over far less powerful Indian ones.   Mr Musk is wide off the mark, not because India does not have oligarchs, but because the primary resistance to Starlink is not being driven by Mukesh Ambani of Jio or Sunil Mittal of Bharti Airtel, India’s telecom biggies, but the Government of India itself. The government is seriously concerned about the security ramifications of handing out satphones by the thousand to entities that could prove to be inimical to India.   Mr Musk may recall that when Starlink announced its intention to offer services in India, the first partners to tie up with him were the very same oligarchs he now rails against. The Modi government, to prevent a duopoly, has paid out or written off hundreds of crores in order to keep both Bharat Sanchar Nigam and Vodafone alive. If Mr Musk were really keen to serve the last man in India’s far-flung areas, he could easily have bailed out Vodafone himself and entrenched himself in the Indian telecom woodwork. But he didn’t. He wants to enter the Indian market both to make money and build political heft. With X, Grok (his artificial intelligence arm) and Starlink, he would be in a very powerful position to influence Indian politics.  The reality is that the overall market for satellite communications is likely to be very small initially. The official reason for allowing foreign satcom players to offer services in India is that regular telecom services in India’s interior and hilly regions are either poor or non-existent. But if one assumes that the people in these regions are also relatively poor, the paying market for such services is likely to be weak too — at least in the initial years.  The real market for satellite communication services (which include direct-to-phone internet services via satellite) will come in the following order: The state (armed forces, central and state police, administrators), followed by  politicians, businessmen, the urban rich and middle classes. The last four, mostly urban dwellers, do not need satphones when broadband Wi-Fi and 5G are already available to them.  For this category of potential users, a satphone would substantially be a vanity purchase like iPhones or folding mobile phones. But we cannot fail to add the one category that would want satphones as of yesterday: Smugglers and anti-social elements. So the pretence that satellite phones will be used to serve poor Arunachal goatherds is laughable. The rich always make their case by riding on the logic of helping the poor. Mr Musk is not going to give the Ladakhi citizen a satphone at  ₹199 a month rental.   The second reason why the oligarch argument does not quite hold is that the upfront investment in the business is huge. Both Sunil Mittal and Mukesh Ambani would have liked to ride on Mr Musk’s coattails rather than make those investments themselves. On the other hand, it was the government that nudged Mr Ambani to put up 1,600 near-Earth satellites in order to offer a home-grown alternative before Mr Musk wades in with his big bucks. The delays are probably deliberate on the government’s part, because it does not want Starlink to become so powerful in India before the domestic alternatives are made available. It is not the oligarchs who may be stalling Starlink, but the sovereign, which worries about internal and external security.  While Starlink has announced that it will comply with India’s security concerns, Mr Musk is a loose cannon with huge political opinions and interests. His Starlink has played a crucial role in the Ukraine-Russia war on the side of the former, and has even been known to pull services to Russians close to the warfront. He backs many Conservative and Right-wing governments in Europe and Latin America, including the now surging Alternative for Germany.   He was vociferous in demanding Keir Starmer’s resignation, and calling for a general election in the United Kingdom in January 2025. Mr Musk played a crucial role in consolidating the forces supporting Donald Trump in the 2024 Presidential elections, and it was only after he fell out with Mr Trump that his power in Washington ebbed. But in terms of money clout, he is George Soros raised to the power of 10: A businessman with the money and the intent to meddle in the politics of other countries.  Given the United States’ new-found willingness to slow down India’s economic rise and impede its ability to export more goods and services to America, there is no saying when Mr Musk will be used to needle and deter India. In fact, Mr Musk’s statement on oligarchs may make any Indian concessions to him on Starlink improbable. India has good reason to keep him away as long as possible.  India’s security concerns are real. Only anarchists will argue otherwise. There is a lot of political churn happening in India, and several sections of society are on the streets for various reasons (opposition parties, farmers, students, quota activists). The police forces in various states often use internet shutdowns to prevent rioting mobs from communicating with one another and making policing impossible. The easy availability of satphones with internet connections would make this method of crowd control impossible.   Also, the borders in the north and east are unstable, with large tribal and other populations freely moving across the Myanmar border. The availability of satphones in the hands of insurgents is a threat India cannot take lightly, and if we add the possibility of a politically-minded Starlink boss capable of using his power to impact politics in various countries, the delay in granting security clearance to Starlink is not difficult to understand.  There is a good case for satellite phones being totally in the hands of Indian businessmen who are subject to Indian laws and amenable to sovereign pressure to avoid aiding a breakdown in law and order or helping anti-social elements and insurgents. Keeping Elon Musk out would be an act of sovereign power, not oligarchic pressure. In this writer’s opinion, Mr Musk should never get a satellite licence in India.

entry.title: The world is not the map
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The world is not the mapThe world is not the map

A UN-backed push for more accurate world maps highlights how every map involves compromises-and how the way we depict the Earth can shape our view of the world

premium

Africa is about 14 times larger than Greenland, a difference obscured by the commonly used Mercator map projection(Image: Wikimedia Commons)

Atanu Biswas5 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTWhile the Earth might be round, the map hanging on my wall is most definitely not. This seemingly innocent observation now has a fresh lease of political life. The United Nations General Assembly endorsed on September 4 an African-led resolution endorsing world maps depicting continents’ sizes proportionally more accurately. It, however, doesn’t ban Mercator projections nor mandate any other form of maps. It merely promotes the greater use of equal area maps, such as Equal Earth maps, especially when it comes to size representation.  The map that we grew up looking at doesn’t only show us locations of countries on Earth but also shapes our view of the world itself. But, let’s take an orange, peel it off delicately, and attempt to flatten all the peel out onto a tabletop. It wrinkles, rips, overlaps, or stretches. This simple experiment illustrates the problem of map-making from its beginning. The Earth is a curve, whereas paper is flat. One can cut and reassemble the peel, but cannot flatten it out completely without some modification. This phenomenon can be described in a reversed way, too: Try to cover an orange by a flat sheet of paper without distortion. Failure to do it doesn’t depend on the paper, but on geometry.  Nearly 200 years ago, in 1827, the legendary German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss offered a mathematical explanation to this problem by his Theorema Egregium. The curvature of the sphere is positive, and that of the plane is zero. Their geometrical natures are clearly different. Hence, while we project Earth, we have to give up something. We can keep form, area, some distance, or directions on our map. But we cannot keep all of them. There’s no ideal world map — that’s not a defect of cartography, but the effect of mathematics.  The map most of us use was invented by Gerardus Mercator in 1569. This map was extremely successful because of its practical uses — it was used for navigation as it preserved angles. In terms of its goal, it was an amazing creation. But Mercator has its noticeable drawback — sizes of objects become more and more exaggerated towards the poles. Take Greenland, which seems nearly the same size as Africa. It isn’t. Africa is actually 14 times larger. However, oddly enough, a projection intended for seafarers became the default map of the world in textbooks and also in practice.  An equal-area projection alters this perspective. Though, it doesn’t solve the problem from a mathematical standpoint. It just makes another kind of compromise. The Gall-Peters map preserves area but changes shape. Winkel Tripel tries to reduce multiple distortions. Though Goode Homolosine map projection maintains the proportion of sizes, the oceans have been split into pieces on the map. Equal Earth Projection was created by Tom Patterson, Bojan Savrič, and Bernhard Jenny in 2018. It retains relative size and maintains continent shape.  Which map, therefore, is the right one? Well, correct for what? A sailor would use one map, while a geographer would require another. A geography textbook will have yet another preference. Each map is an expression of the decision made on what to preserve and what to sacrifice.  However, each map is made with certain decisions in mind. Why is north at the top? Why is Europe in the middle? Why is the Pacific always shown on the margins? Nature doesn’t demand that “north” always be placed “up.” An upside-down map makes Australia appear at the top. Centre the Pacific, and the division between East and West starts looking like something completely different. The Earth remains the same. All that has changed is the frame around the picture. A map might begin geometrically, but it can become political.  Certainly one of the finest instances where humanity plays with the world is demonstrated in the movie The Great Dictator (1940) in which Charlie Chaplin played the Hitler-like character Adenoid Hynkel. In the film, Hynkel takes a globe, blows it up, and starts playing with it, throwing it up in the air. For a moment, the whole world is his toy. Then it bursts. While the sequence is comedic, there’s something strangely fitting about imagining the scene in relation to mapping. A globe keeps the curvature of the Earth; a map takes it away. Once the world is flattened, however, it becomes easier to reshape — shift boundaries, change centres, adjust scales. Maps have their own kind of power.  We shouldn’t, however, throw Mercator’s map in the dustbin of history. It still has its uses — for navigation and otherwise — wherever its attributes come in handy. Neither do we want to think that Equal Earth provides the solution. No map does so. Perhaps the truly honest answer is to appreciate the compromises in any map. This, perhaps, is the real message of the UN’s map debate. The earth will continue on just where it was before — round, huge, and completely unconcerned with the squabbles of the map-makers.

entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Best of Opinion: Central banks need to be ready for geopolitical risksBest of Opinion: Central banks need to be ready for geopolitical risks

From integrated transport planning and uncertainty over Rodtep to the RBI's geopolitical challenges, family business governance, today's opinions examine policy and institutional reform

The Reserve Bank of India needs to plan ahead for geopolitical tensions

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page.  The Union Cabinet’s approval of an Integrated Transport & Logistics Authority is a welcome step towards ending fragmented planning across roads, railways, ports, aviation, waterways, and urban transport. Today’s first editorial notes that ITLA will prepare a long-term National Transport Master Plan, appraise major projects, monitor implementation, and create a unified transport data repository. Integrated planning could improve capital allocation, reduce duplication, and lower logistics costs, but the authority must have sufficient influence over project selection and investment priorities. Duplication with PM Gati Shakti must also be avoided, while data integration requires interoperability and safeguards. ITLA should ultimately be judged by whether planning changes implementation. The government’s three-month extension of Rodtep provides continuity but little certainty for exporters, who finalise orders well in advance. Keeping existing rates and value caps unchanged does not address concerns arising from the scheme’s uncertain future and sharply lower budget allocation. The second editorial notes that Rodtep refunds embedded taxes rather than providing a conventional export subsidy, making predictability essential for competitiveness. Previous policy changes, including rate restrictions and subsequent restoration, have highlighted the costs of volatility. With exports gaining momentum, the editorial urges a longer extension, greater funding, consultation, a defined transition period, and policy stability to support exporters. The Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) delayed rate hike has left it confronting higher oil prices, surplus liquidity, rising US Treasury yields, narrowing India-US bond spreads, and renewed FII outflows. T T Ram Mohan contends that the central bank should have acted earlier, while arguing that conventional monetary policy frameworks are inadequate in a world where geopolitical disruptions are increasingly routine. He proposes creating a Strategic Affairs unit within the RBI that would bring together expertise in international relations, defence, energy, and economics. Such an unit would assess geopolitical developments, construct scenarios for oil prices, inflation, and exchange rates, and assign probabilities to them, enabling better-informed decisions. India’s family-owned businesses face a new governance challenge: control can now be contested from within, rather than threatened by outside acquirers. Amit Tandon uses the Tata Sons dispute to suggest that promoter stakes may no longer guarantee boardroom control. Families could respond by retaining executive authority, favouring accommodating directors, strengthening governance charters, and simplifying ownership structures. Yet evidence on family control and performance is mixed, with studies showing that professional managers can outperform family CEOs, while family ownership can support stronger returns. The column concludes that succession planning, governance, professional management, and trust between owners and boards will become crucial. Sebastian Mallaby’s The Infinity Machine offers an extensively researched account of Demis Hassabis, DeepMind, and the quest for superintelligence. In his review of the book,Devangshu Datta traces Hassabis’ extraordinary journey from chess and gaming prodigy to neuroscientist and AI pioneer, highlighting DeepMind’s development of AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and AlphaFold, whose protein-folding breakthrough has accelerated drug research. Mallaby, drawing on hundreds of hours of access to Hassabis and his associates, also chronicles DeepMind’s financial struggles, Google’s acquisition, and Silicon Valley’s corporate rivalries and ethical disputes. Datta praises the book’s meticulous sourcing but finds Mallaby less effective at explaining complex technology and insufficiently critical of Hassabis, suggesting that extraordinary access may have compromised objectivity.
